column1: 1:1|The word of the LORD came to Joel son of Pethuel.|Keeps the brief attribution without adding a reign or date absent from the source.

1:2|Hear this, elders!
Listen, everyone living in the land!
Has anything like this happened in your days
or in the days of your ancestors?|Retains the two audiences and the unprecedented-event question.

1:3|Tell your children about it;\nlet your children tell their children,\nand their children the generation after them.|Preserves the four-generation transmission instead of shortening it to a general remembrance.

1:4|What the cutting locust left, the swarming locust ate.\nWhat the swarming locust left, the creeping locust ate.\nWhat the creeping locust left, the stripping locust ate.|Keeps all four Hebrew locust terms and the three repeated consumption clauses; labels are descriptive, not a biological claim.

1:5|Wake up, drunkards, and weep!
Wail, all you wine drinkers,
for the sweet wine
has been cut off from your mouths.|Retains the specific addressees and the mouth image rather than generic economic loss.

1:6|A nation has come up against my land,
powerful and beyond counting.
Its teeth are a lion’s teeth;
it has the fangs of a lioness.|Preserves nation and predatory teeth while leaving the locust/army imagery intertwined.

1:7|It has devastated my vine
and stripped my fig tree bare.
It has peeled it completely and thrown it aside;
its branches have turned white.|Keeps the possessive landowner voice and the visible whiteness of stripped branches.
1:8|Lament like a young woman clothed in sackcloth\nfor the husband of her youth.|Retains the bereaved young woman and husband relationship, with betrothed possibility in notes.

1:9|Grain offering and drink offering
have been cut off from the house of the LORD.
The priests mourn,
those who serve the LORD.|Preserves both offerings and both divine-name occurrences.

1:10|The fields are devastated;
the ground mourns.
Grain is devastated,
new wine has dried up, and oil has failed.|Keeps the personified ground and repeated devastation before the three produce losses.

1:11|Be ashamed, farmers!
Wail, vine growers,
for the wheat and barley,
because the harvest of the fields is lost.|Preserves shame/drying wordplay as shame here and keeps both crops.

1:12|The vine has dried up;
the fig tree has withered.
Pomegranate, palm, and apple—
all the trees of the field have dried up.
Joy itself has dried up among human beings.|Retains the full tree list and repeated drying that culminates in human joy.

1:13|Put on sackcloth and lament, priests!
Wail, you who serve at the altar!
Come, spend the night in sackcloth,
you who serve my God,
for grain offering and drink offering
are withheld from the house of your God.|Keeps nightlong mourning and the my/your God shift.

1:14|Set apart a fast;
call a solemn assembly.
Gather the elders and everyone living in the land
to the house of the LORD your God,
and cry out to the LORD.|Preserves the coordinated communal actions and twice-named recipient.
1:15|Alas for the day!\nThe day of the LORD is near;\nit comes like devastation from the Almighty.|Keeps the shod/Shaddai connection through devastation/Almighty explained in the note.
1:16|Has not food been cut off before our eyes,\nand joy and celebration\nfrom the house of our God?|Maintains the rhetorical question and parallel loss of food and worship's joy.

1:17|Seeds shrivel beneath the clods.
Storehouses stand deserted;
granaries are torn down,
for the grain has dried up.|Chooses the common contextual sense of three rare opening words while explicitly flagging their uncertainty.

1:18|How the animals groan!
Herds of cattle wander in distress
because they have no pasture.
Even the flocks of sheep suffer.|Preserves cattle and sheep and their suffering without attributing moral guilt to the animals.
1:19|To you, LORD, I cry,\nfor fire has consumed the wilderness pastures\nand flame has burned all the trees of the field.|Keeps the first-person prayer and parallel fire/flame devastation.
1:20|Even the wild animals pant toward you,\nfor the streambeds have dried up\nand fire has consumed the wilderness pastures.|Preserves animal appeal to God and the repeated pasture clause.

2:1|Blow the ram’s horn in Zion!
Sound the alarm on my holy mountain!
Let everyone living in the land tremble,
for the day of the LORD is coming; it is near.|Retains abrupt divine my within the call and repeats the near-day announcement.

2:2|A day of darkness and gloom,
a day of cloud and thick darkness!
Like dawn spreading over the mountains
comes a vast and powerful people.
Nothing like it has ever been,
nor will be again for generations to come.|Keeps dawn rather than silently making it darkness and preserves unparalleled scale.
2:4|They look like horses;\nthey run like cavalry.|Keeps comparisons rather than identifying the creatures as literal horsemen.

2:5|With a sound like chariots they leap over the mountaintops,\nlike the crackle of flame consuming stubble,\nlike a powerful people drawn up for battle.|Retains all three similes and the audible quality of the invasion.
2:6|Peoples writhe before them;\nevery face loses its color.|Chooses pallor for the uncertain facial expression while noting darkening as alternative.

2:7|They run like warriors
and scale a wall like soldiers.
Each keeps to its own path;
they do not swerve from their routes.|Preserves ordered movement and the repeated military comparisons.

2:8|They do not jostle one another;
each moves in its own lane.
They plunge through the weapons
and are not stopped.|Keeps the difficult weapon phrase as penetration despite resistance, without asserting literal invulnerability.

2:9|They rush upon the city,
run along the wall,
climb into the houses,
and enter through the windows like a thief.|Preserves the four escalating locations and final thief simile.

2:10|Before them the earth shakes
and the heavens tremble.
Sun and moon grow dark;
the stars withdraw their light.|Keeps cosmic response and literal celestial subjects rather than explaining an eclipse.

2:11|The LORD raises his voice before his army.
His camp is vast;
powerful is the one who carries out his word.
The day of the LORD is great and deeply terrifying—
who can endure it?|Maintains divine command, army, and the unanswered endurance question.
2:12|“Even now,” declares the LORD,\n“return to me with all your heart,\nwith fasting, weeping, and mourning.”|Keeps even now as the interruption of judgment and the full threefold response.

2:13|Tear your hearts, not your clothes,
and return to the LORD your God.
He is gracious and compassionate,
slow to anger and rich in faithful love,
and he relents from bringing disaster.|Retains the bodily/clothing contrast and all attributes; disaster avoids confusing raah with moral evil here.

2:14|Who knows? He may turn and relent
and leave a blessing behind him—
a grain offering and a drink offering
for the LORD your God.|Preserves uncertainty rather than turning repentance into a guaranteed outcome.
2:15|Blow the ram’s horn in Zion!\nSet apart a fast;\ncall a solemn assembly.|Repeats the horn call and earlier assembly instructions exactly for recognition.

2:17|Between the porch and the altar,
let the priests who serve the LORD weep.
Let them say, “Spare your people, LORD.
Do not make your inheritance a disgrace,
for nations to rule over them.
Why should the peoples say, ‘Where is their God?’”|Follows rule-over sense of mashal while noting proverbial taunt alternative; preserves architectural location.
2:18|Then the LORD became zealous for his land\nand had compassion on his people.|Uses narrative past for the wayyiqtol turn without inventing an intervening repentance scene.

2:19|The LORD answered his people:
“I am sending you grain, new wine, and oil,
and you will have enough.
I will no longer make you a disgrace among the nations.|Keeps the restored three provisions and the reversal of public shame.

2:20|I will drive the northern one far from you
and thrust it into a dry, desolate land,
its front into the eastern sea
and its rear into the western sea.
Its stench will rise, its foul smell will go up,
for it has done great things.”|Leaves northern one unidentified and retains front/rear, two seas, and the ambiguous great deeds.
2:21|Do not fear, ground!\nCelebrate and rejoice,\nfor the LORD has done great things.|Repeats great things with a new subject and addresses the ground itself.

2:22|Do not fear, wild animals,
for the wilderness pastures are green.
The trees bear fruit;
fig tree and vine give their full yield.|Keeps animals as direct addressees and reverses the earlier vegetation loss.

2:23|Children of Zion, celebrate and rejoice
in the LORD your God.
He has given you the autumn rain in righteousness;
he sends rain down for you,
autumn and spring rain as before.|Chooses rain in agricultural context, preserving righteousness and noting teacher and first-month alternatives.
2:24|The threshing floors will be full of grain;\nthe vats will overflow with new wine and oil.|Keeps the produce and processing locations paired rather than generic abundance.

2:25|“I will repay you for the years eaten by
the swarming locust, the creeping locust,
the stripping locust, and the cutting locust—
my great army that I sent against you.|Retains all four terms in this verse's different order and explicitly divine agency.

2:26|You will eat your fill
and praise the name of the LORD your God,
who has done wonders for you.
My people will never again be put to shame.|Preserves satiation, praise, and the full no-shame promise.

2:27|You will know that I am among Israel,\nthat I am the LORD your God and there is no other.\nMy people will never again be put to shame.|Repeats the promise unchanged and retains presence plus exclusivity.
2:29|Even on male and female slaves\nI will pour out my Spirit in those days.|Makes enslavement explicit and preserves both sexes without adding my from a later quotation.
2:30|I will display wonders in the heavens and on earth:\nblood, fire, and columns of smoke.|Preserves the three signs without assigning a modern event.
2:31|The sun will turn to darkness\nand the moon to blood\nbefore the great and terrifying day of the LORD comes.|Keeps the cosmic transformations and before relationship.

2:32|Everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will escape,
for on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be deliverance,
as the LORD has said,
and among the survivors will be those the LORD calls.|Preserves both human calling and divine calling and all three name occurrences.
3:1|“In those days and at that time,\nwhen I restore the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem,|Follows the read restore form and carries the temporal clause into the next verse.

3:2|I will gather all the nations
and bring them down to the Valley of Jehoshaphat.
There I will enter into judgment with them
for my people, my inheritance Israel,
whom they scattered among the nations.
They divided up my land.|Keeps the judgment setting, scattered people, and divided land as distinct charges.
3:3|They cast lots for my people,\ntraded a boy for a prostitute,\nand sold a girl for wine and drank it.|Preserves the sex and age of the trafficked children and the explicit transactions.

3:4|And what have you against me, Tyre and Sidon
and all the regions of Philistia?
Are you repaying me for something?
If you are paying me back,
I will swiftly bring your repayment down on your own heads.|Keeps the repeated repayment root and named coastal regions.
3:5|You took my silver and gold\nand carried my finest treasures into your temples.|Preserves divine ownership and the destination, noting temple/palace range if needed.
3:6|You sold the people of Judah and Jerusalem to the Greeks\nto send them far from their own territory.|Keeps the named buyers and removal purpose without importing a conquest date.
3:7|Look, I will rouse them from the place where you sold them\nand bring your repayment down on your own heads.|Repeats the retribution clause and the victims' awakening from sale.

3:8|I will sell your sons and daughters
into the hands of the people of Judah,
and they will sell them to the Sabeans, a distant nation.”
For the LORD has spoken.|Preserves the disturbing retaliatory enslavement and specific buyers without editorial endorsement.

3:9|Proclaim this among the nations:\n“Consecrate a war! Rouse the warriors!\nLet all the soldiers approach and advance.|Retains consecration rather than merely preparation and the repeated mobilization.

3:10|Beat your plowshares into swords\nand your pruning hooks into spears.\nLet the weak say, ‘I am a warrior!’|Keeps the deliberate reversal of agricultural peace imagery and the weak fighter's boast.
3:11|Hurry and come, all you surrounding nations;\ngather there!”\nBring down your warriors, LORD!|Marks the shift from nations' summons to prayer without merging the two armies.

3:12|“Let the nations rouse themselves
and come up to the Valley of Jehoshaphat,
for there I will sit to judge
all the surrounding nations.|Preserves divine first-person judicial seating and repeated location.

3:13|Swing the sickle, for the harvest is ripe.
Come, tread, for the winepress is full;
the vats overflow,
for their evil is great.”|Keeps harvest and vintage as judgment imagery with evil as explicit explanation.

3:14|Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of decision!\nThe day of the LORD is near\nin the valley of decision.|Repeats multitudes and valley; note clarifies divine verdict rather than an invitation to human decision.
3:15|Sun and moon grow dark;\nthe stars withdraw their light.|Matches the recurring cosmic-darkness clause for literary recognition.

3:16|The LORD roars from Zion
and raises his voice from Jerusalem;
heaven and earth shake.
But the LORD is a refuge for his people,
a stronghold for the people of Israel.|Keeps threatening roar alongside refuge and both divine-name occurrences.

3:17|“You will know that I am the LORD your God,
dwelling in Zion, my holy mountain.
Jerusalem will be holy,
and strangers will no longer pass through her.|Retains strangers rather than silently restricting to invaders; explains hostile context in a note.

3:18|On that day the mountains will drip sweet wine,
the hills will flow with milk,
and all Judah’s streambeds will flow with water.
A spring will flow from the house of the LORD
and water the Valley of Acacias.|Preserves abundant liquids and the sanctuary spring without forcing a geographical identification.

3:19|Egypt will become a desolation,
and Edom a desolate wilderness,
for violence against the people of Judah,
whose innocent blood they shed in their land.|Retains both nations and bloodshed as the reason, with possessive land ambiguity noted.
3:20|But Judah will be inhabited forever,\nand Jerusalem through every generation.|Keeps enduring habitation distinct from a modern political application.

3:21|I will clear their bloodguilt that I have not cleared.”\nThe LORD dwells in Zion.|Follows the pinned clear/acquit verb, noting vindicate/avenge readings and leaving the blood's referent cautious.
